title: Turn a Handwritten Grocery List Into a Shared Digital List
description: A practical way to photograph a paper grocery list, check the recognized items and share the final list with your household.
body_markdown:
## Start with a photo that is easy to read

Paper grocery lists are fast to write, but they can be hard to share. Take a photo with the whole list in the frame, keep the page flat, and avoid shadows from your hand or phone. Handwriting recognition is never perfect, so a review step matters more than a flashy instant result.

## Check every recognized product

Look carefully at names, quantities, and units. If the paper only says *milk*, the application should not claim you wrote *two litres of milk*. Leave the quantity unspecified until you choose one. Where an item is unreadable, the safer result is a review warning—not an invented product.

## Keep groceries separate from inventory

A list tells your household what you intend to buy. It doesn't prove the groceries are already in your kitchen. Imported items should land in a **To Buy** shopping list until somebody confirms the purchase.

## Make the list useful to everyone

Group duplicates, confirm unusual products, and share the resulting list with the people who shop with you. Before heading to the store, check what is already at home to avoid buying another package unnecessarily.

## Try the workflow with GHM

GHM's [handwritten grocery list scanner](/handwritten-grocery-list-scanner) is designed for printed or handwritten lists. Review what was recognized and select an existing shopping list or create a new one before saving. The app may struggle with unclear handwriting, so always verify the results.

title: How to Split Grocery Bills Fairly With Roommates
description: A repeatable system for separating shared groceries from personal purchases and keeping reimbursements understandable.
body_markdown:
## Decide what counts as shared before shopping

The biggest source of roommate confusion is often not the total bill; it is whether a specific item belongs to everyone. Agree on a short list of shared essentials such as cooking oil, cleaning products or milk. Keep personal snacks or dietary-specific products separate.

## Record who actually paid

When someone pays for a mixed grocery trip, keep the receipt and note the payer. Enter the full amount once, then assign only the shared portion to the people who agreed to split it. Do not divide personal products equally by default.

## Choose a fair method for each expense

Equal splits are easy for common supplies. Custom splits are better if a product benefits some roommates more than others or if one roommate is away for part of the month. Make the method visible so everyone can understand the total.

## Settle on a predictable schedule

Weekly or monthly reimbursement is usually simpler than transferring money after every purchase. Keep a single ledger of who owes and who is owed. When someone pays back a balance, record the reimbursement so it does not keep appearing as unpaid.

## A simple example

If a grocery receipt includes shared staples and one person's personal groceries, subtract the personal items first. Split the shared amount only among participants. The personal portion belongs to the person who bought it, regardless of who paid at checkout.

## Use a shared household record

A tool like GHM's [household expenses](/household-expenses) can link expense records with shopping and receipts. The essential habit is still transparency: agree on rules first, then let the software keep the arithmetic organized.

title: How to Track Pantry Inventory Without a Spreadsheet
description: A low-effort inventory method for knowing what you have, avoiding duplicates and tracking products as they are used.
body_markdown:
## Don't begin by cataloguing your entire house

Start with the food you frequently run out of or accidentally buy twice: rice, flour, canned goods, frozen vegetables and household supplies. Recording a small, accurate set is better than maintaining a giant list that nobody updates.

## Use units that reflect how you actually shop

Choose units that make sense: pieces for unopened cans, kilograms for bulk rice, or packages for wrapped items. Avoid mixing pieces and kilograms for the same product unless you can state a reliable conversion.

## Connect new shopping to inventory

When you complete a shopping trip, confirm what was purchased before increasing stock quantities. A planned grocery list isn't an inventory transaction. Check receipt quantities, especially for produce sold by weight.

## Set realistic low-stock signals

For a staple used every week, low stock might mean one unopened package remains. For an occasional ingredient, the same quantity could be plenty. Review thresholds after a few normal shopping trips rather than trying to predict everything on day one.

## Keep people involved without making extra work

In a shared home, everyone should see the same available inventory. Make corrections straightforward when someone uses an item or when a scan identifies the wrong product.

## Use what you have before buying more

Check inventory while planning dinner and before sending someone to the store. GHM combines [shared household inventory](/shared-households) with [meal planning](/meal-planning), so missing ingredients can move to a grocery list after review.

title: How to Plan Dinner Using Ingredients Already at Home
description: A straightforward cook-from-home system that reduces duplicate shopping and turns recipe shortages into a focused grocery list.
body_markdown:
## Start with what needs to be used

Open your fridge and pantry, and make a short list of ingredients that should be used soon. Check actual freshness and food safety rather than relying only on an app's estimated expiry date.

## Choose a meal around two or three main ingredients

If you have potatoes, peas and flour, you might make a simple stuffed flatbread or vegetable dish. If you have lentils and rice, a one-pot meal may fit. It is easier to pick meals from ingredients you already own than to shop for a long recipe from scratch.

## Adapt to your household's dietary needs

Check allergies, vegetarian requirements and whether your family avoids onion or garlic. A recipe suggestion should be adjustable, not treated as an instruction to buy ingredients that you never use.

## Separate essentials from optional additions

Salt, oil and spices matter, but your household may already have plenty. Mark optional garnishes and substitutions clearly. Review the shortage list before adding anything to shopping.

## Scale servings before shopping

A recipe for two should not automatically create a four-person shopping list. Confirm servings, then check each ingredient amount against what's available. For weighted produce, keep the units consistent.

## Share the plan

A good meal workflow lets someone choose dinner while another person buys the few missing items. Explore [GHM meal planning](/meal-planning) and use its inventory-aware suggestions as a starting point; always verify availability.

title: How to Organize Grocery Receipts and Track Spending
description: A practical receipt-review routine for tracking food costs, inventory updates and shared household expenses.
body_markdown:
## Keep one dependable record of grocery purchases

Grocery spending becomes difficult to understand when receipts are scattered across photos, bags and bank statements. Capture them soon after shopping and keep the store, date and final total together.

## Review scanned receipt data

Receipt OCR can misread weights, discounts, multi-buy promotions and similar-looking product names. Check the total and individual amounts before accepting a scan. A receipt with an incorrect total will distort spending reports.

## Distinguish unit price from final line price

Bulk products may be sold by weight, while packaged items use pieces or packages. Record both the unit and quantity when available. Do not treat a per-kilogram price as the amount actually paid.

## Link purchases to inventory only after approval

Updating inventory from a receipt is useful, but only if products and quantities are correct. Unrecognized items should be editable, and duplicate products should be matched carefully before stock is increased.

## Track categories over time

Compare monthly grocery spending, but remember that a large stock-up trip may shift purchases between months. Use several months of history instead of treating one expensive week as proof something is wrong.

## Handle household payments separately

Who purchased food and who ultimately owes for it are different questions. If roommates split a receipt, keep a separate reimbursement record.

title: How to Share Grocery Lists With Family and Avoid Double Buying
description: Simple habits for a live family shopping list that everyone can trust at the store.
body_markdown:
## Keep one list for the trip

A family can end up with grocery items in text messages, notebook pages and multiple phone notes. Choose one shared list that everyone can check and edit, including while shopping.

## Decide who can add and finish items

For ordinary groceries, simple shared editing usually works. If someone is planning an expensive stock-up or buying for a special event, agree on who reviews the final list.

## Mark shopping progress clearly

Distinguish **To Buy** from items already in the cart and purchases that are actually complete. Marking an item as bought before checkout can mislead other family members.

## Use quantities and store preferences

A list item such as *bread* may be too vague. Add the amount or preferred type when it matters. Keep preferences flexible if the store is out of stock, and confirm substitutions before changing the family's inventory.

## Check what is at home first

Before adding milk or detergent, check existing inventory. Shared lists work best when they connect to a shared view of what is already in the house.

## Prepare for an unreliable signal

Stores sometimes have poor reception. Make sure whoever is shopping can still access a practical version of the list, and avoid assuming that delayed updates have already synced.
